Now, I want to focus on a principle that has been with us since the early days of web development but has been largely forgotten in the modern era: progressive enhancement.

entry.title: The CSS Conundrum: Why Utility Classes Are Not The Answer

link.title: The CSS Conundrum: Why Utility Classes Are Not The Answer

entry.content:
In the previous articles in this series, I’ve examined how modern web development has drifted from its foundational principles and advocated for a return to HyperText. Now it’s time to address another concerning trend: the proliferation of utility-first CSS frameworks, particularly TailwindCSS, and the practice of embedding styling directly within component markup.

The Rise of Utility Classes

The popularity of utility-first CSS frameworks didn’t emerge from nowhere. Traditional CSS approaches presented genuine challenges:

  1. Global scope leading to specificity conflicts
  2. The cascade creating unexpected side effects
  3. Difficulty in maintaining large stylesheets
  4. Challenges in creating reusable styles

These were legitimate problems that needed solving. But as with JavaScript frameworks, I would argue that the solution has introduced more problems than it solved.

The TailwindCSS Phenomenon

TailwindCSS has become extraordinarily popular, particularly among developers working with component-based frameworks. The premise is straightforward: rather than creating semantic class names that describe the element’s purpose, you apply tiny single-purpose utility classes directly to your HTML elements:

<button class="bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white font-bold py-2 px-4 rounded">
  Click me
</button>

Proponents argue this approach:

  1. Eliminates the need to context-switch between HTML and CSS files
  2. Reduces the risk of unused CSS accumulating
  3. Makes it easy to understand exactly what styles are applied
  4. Enables rapid prototyping and consistent design

At first glance, these benefits seem compelling. But they come at significant costs.

The Problems with Utility Classes

Readability and Semantics

HTML was designed to be semantic—to convey meaning about content structure. CSS was designed to separate presentation from that structure. Utility classes fundamentally break this separation, resulting in markup like this:

<div class="flex flex-col md:flex-row justify-between items-center p-4 bg-gray-100 rounded-lg shadow-md">
  <div class="flex items-center mb-4 md:mb-0">
    <img class="w-10 h-10 rounded-full mr-4" src="avatar.jpg" alt="User avatar">
    <div>
      <h3 class="text-lg font-medium text-gray-900">User Name</h3>
      <p class="text-sm text-gray-500">User Title</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <button class="bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white font-bold py-2 px-4 rounded">
    Follow
  </button>
</div>

What is this component? A user card? A comment? A notification? The HTML provides no semantic clues because it’s overwhelmed with presentation details.

Compare this to semantic HTML with separate CSS:

<div class="user-card">
  <div class="user-profile">
    <img class="avatar" src="avatar.jpg" alt="User avatar">
    <div class="user-info">
      <h3 class="name">User Name</h3>
      <p class="title">User Title</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <button class="follow-button">Follow</button>
</div>

The second example clearly communicates what each element represents. A developer can immediately understand the component’s purpose without needing to mentally parse dozens of utility classes.

Maintainability

While component-based frameworks mitigate some of the maintainability issues, utility classes create new ones:

  1. Changes require markup updates across many files: If your design system changes (e.g., standard button padding increases), you must update every component rather than changing one CSS rule.

  2. Responsive designs become unwieldy: Notice the md:flex-row and md:mb-0 classes in the example. As breakpoints multiply, these conditional classes create significant visual noise.

  3. Duplication abounds: The same combinations of utility classes appear repeatedly throughout the codebase, often with subtle variations that create inconsistency.

The False Promise of Colocation

Utility-first approaches are often justified by the desire to keep everything related to a component in one file. But this “colocation” actually creates tighter coupling and makes systemic changes more difficult.

When styling is embedded directly in markup:

  1. Global styling changes become nearly impossible: There’s no single place to update a component style across the application.

  2. Design system consistency suffers: Even with disciplined developers, variations inevitably creep in when styles are repeated rather than referenced.

  3. The cascade—one of CSS’s most powerful features—is nullified: Instead of leveraging inheritance, styles are explicitly repeated at every level.

The Spirit of CSS

To understand why utility classes represent such a departure, we need to revisit CSS’s core principles:

  1. Separation of concerns: CSS was explicitly designed to separate presentation from content, allowing each to evolve independently.

  2. The cascade: The “C” in CSS stands for “Cascading,” allowing styles to flow through the document tree and be selectively overridden.

  3. Inheritance: Child elements inherit properties from their parents, reducing repetition and creating visual consistency.

  4. Specificity: A sophisticated system for resolving competing style rules based on selector types.

Utility classes effectively abandon these principles in favour of a more programmatic, inline approach to styling. This isn’t enhancing CSS—it’s replacing it with a fundamentally different paradigm.

A More Balanced Approach

I’m not suggesting we return to massive global stylesheets with selector specificity wars. But there are better alternatives than saturating our markup with utility classes:

  1. CSS Modules: Scoped CSS files that eliminate global namespace concerns whilst maintaining the separation of concerns.

  2. SASS/SCSS with sensible organization: Preprocessors with partials, variables, and mixins provide modularity without abandoning CSS principles.

  3. Custom Properties (CSS Variables): Modern CSS includes powerful variable capabilities that enable consistent design tokens.

  4. Well-structured BEM methodology: The Block-Element-Modifier pattern creates namespaced classes that clearly communicate component structure.

These approaches maintain the separation of concerns whilst addressing the legitimate problems that led to utility-first CSS.

Conclusion

The web was built on the principle that content, presentation, and behaviour should be separate concerns. HTML provides structure, CSS provides presentation, and JavaScript provides behaviour. This separation isn’t arbitrary—it allows each layer to evolve independently and excel at its primary purpose.

Utility-first CSS frameworks like Tailwind, encouraged by component-based JavaScript frameworks, have blurred these boundaries, embedding presentation deeply into content markup. While this approach may offer short-term convenience for individual developers, it creates long-term maintainability problems and undermines the web’s fundamental architecture.

Like the overuse of JavaScript and the artificial division between frontend and backend, the proliferation of utility classes represents another way our industry has drifted from the web’s foundational principles.

In the next article, I’ll explore potential topics like accessible progressive enhancement, the return of server-side rendering with frameworks like Phoenix LiveView and Laravel Livewire, or the evolving role of JavaScript in a HyperText-centric world. I welcome your feedback on which direction would be most valuable to explore.
entry.summary: In the previous articles in this series, I’ve examined how modern web development has drifted from its foundational principles and advocated for a return to HyperText. Now it’s time to address another concerning trend: the proliferation of utility-first CSS frameworks, particularly TailwindCSS, and the practice of embedding styling directly within component markup.

entry.title: HyperText and HTML: Why SPAs Are Dead

link.title: HyperText and HTML: Why SPAs Are Dead

entry.content:
In the first article of this series, I established my position that modern web development has strayed from its roots, creating unnecessary complexity and artificial divisions. Now, I want to focus specifically on how our industry’s obsession with client-side rendering and single-page applications (SPAs) has undermined the very essence of the web: HyperText.

How We Got Here

The rise of SPAs wasn’t arbitrary. Around 2010-2015, several forces converged to make them seem like the logical evolution of web development:

  1. Smartphones created user expectations for app-like experiences
  2. Browser APIs expanded dramatically, enabling more on the client
  3. JavaScript engines became significantly faster
  4. The desire to separate concerns led to API-driven architectures
  5. Facebook’s React introduced a compelling component model

For a time, these applications genuinely solved problems. They provided rich interactions without full page reloads and helped teams scale by separating frontend and backend concerns.

But in solving these problems, we created a host of new ones.

The Price of Client-Side Rendering

The shift to SPAs brought substantial costs that many teams still don’t fully account for:

Complexity

Let’s be frank: modern frontend development is absurdly complex. Consider the toolchain required to build even a simple React application:

  • Webpack (or alternatives) for bundling
  • Babel for transpilation
  • State management libraries (Redux, MobX, Zustand, etc.)
  • Routing libraries
  • Form handling libraries
  • Data fetching utilities
  • Testing frameworks designed specifically for components
  • CSS-in-JS solutions or complex styling approaches

Each of these tools is brilliant in isolation. Webpack, in particular, solves genuinely hard problems. But collectively, they represent an extraordinary amount of complexity—complexity that simply doesn’t exist when rendering HTML on the server.

The JSON API Fallacy

Perhaps the most questionable pattern to emerge is what I call the “JSON API fallacy”: the belief that backends should primarily serve as JSON APIs, even when they have exactly one consumer—the frontend of the same application.

Consider the typical flow in a React application:

  1. Browser loads a minimal HTML shell
  2. JavaScript loads and executes
  3. JavaScript makes API requests to fetch data
  4. JavaScript transforms that data into HTML
  5. The user finally sees content

Compare this to server rendering:

  1. Server processes request
  2. Server generates complete HTML
  3. Browser renders HTML immediately

The SPA approach introduces multiple round trips, client-side processing, and numerous failure modes. All to accomplish what servers have done efficiently for decades: transform data into HTML.

And for what benefit? “Decoupling,” we’re told. But is this decoupling actually serving us?

The Team Silo Problem

This architectural choice directly reinforces the frontend/backend divide I criticised in the first article. With a JSON API between teams, we’ve institutionalised a contract negotiation that must happen before work can proceed.

The backend team builds and documents APIs, the frontend team consumes them, and an enormous amount of communication overhead ensues. When requirements change (as they inevitably do), this process repeats.

Is this really more efficient than having developers who understand both sides?

HTMX: The Return to HyperText

Fortunately, we’re seeing a renaissance of HyperText approaches led by libraries like HTMX. What makes HTMX so compelling is its simplicity: it extends HTML rather than replacing it.

Consider a typical HTMX interaction:

<button hx-post="/submit" hx-target="#response-div">
  Submit
</button>
<div id="response-div"></div>

With just two attributes, we’ve created an asynchronous form submission that updates a specific part of the page. No JSON transformation, no state management, no virtual DOM—just HTML talking to HTML.

HTMX embraces what the web does best: exchanging HTML between client and server. It provides:

  • Partial page updates without full reloads
  • History management and bookmarkable states
  • Form validation and submission
  • Dynamic content loading
  • All with minimal JavaScript

This isn’t a step backward—it’s recognising that HTML was always the right solution for document structure, and enhancing it for modern needs.

The Case Against SPAs

With tools like HTMX available, it’s increasingly difficult to justify SPAs for most web applications. They make sense in specific contexts:

  • Applications with significant offline requirements
  • Highly interactive interfaces like design tools or games
  • Situations where minimising server load is critical

But for the vast majority of CRUD applications, dashboards, content sites, and e-commerce platforms? SPAs represent significant overengineering.

Consider these fundamental questions:

  1. Why generate HTML on the client when servers are designed for this exact purpose?
  2. Why create JSON APIs that will only ever have one consumer?
  3. Why force users to download and execute megabytes of JavaScript before seeing content?
  4. Why rebuild browser features like navigation and form handling in JavaScript?

The Career Question

I anticipate pushback on this idea, largely because many developers have built careers around frontend frameworks. There’s a legitimate concern: if we simplify our approach to web development, what happens to these specialised roles?

This concern reveals an uncomfortable truth: some of the complexity in our industry exists to justify specialisation rather than to solve actual problems.

But I believe this fear is misplaced. Frontend development remains a critical discipline even in a HyperText-centric world:

  • Accessibility requires deep expertise
  • Animation and micro-interactions demand specialisation
  • Performance optimisation is increasingly important
  • CSS layout and responsive design remain challenging
  • Client-side interactivity still has its place

The difference is that frontend developers would focus on these genuinely hard problems rather than reimplementing server rendering on the client.

The Full Stack Future

Moving back toward HyperText doesn’t diminish the role of frontend developers—it elevates all developers to full-stack contributors. When the artificial boundary between frontend and backend dissolves, engineers can:

  • Make end-to-end changes without coordination overhead
  • Understand the full impact of their changes
  • Optimise the entire request/response cycle
  • Create more coherent user experiences

This isn’t just more efficient—it’s more fulfilling work.

Conclusion

SPAs had their moment, and for certain applications, they remain the right choice. But for the vast majority of web projects, it’s time to admit they’ve created more problems than they’ve solved.

By returning to HyperText principles with modern tools like HTMX, we can:

  • Simplify our development process
  • Deliver faster initial page loads
  • Improve accessibility and SEO
  • Reduce development time and costs
  • Create more cohesive teams

The future of web development doesn’t look like ever more complex JavaScript frameworks. It looks like HTML, enhanced with just enough dynamic behaviour to meet modern expectations.

In the next article, I’ll turn my attention to another area where modern practices have arguably gone astray: CSS and the rise of utility-first frameworks like Tailwind.
